CHAPTER 16 - MAGNETIC EFFECT OF ELECTRIC CURRENT

Introduction

For a long time electricity and magnetism were studied as two separate subjects. That changed in 1820 when Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire was deflected. This single observation proved that a moving charge (an electric current) produces a magnetic field, and it launched the whole subject of electromagnetism. In this chapter we build the quantitative laws that describe the magnetic field of a current (the Biot-Savart law and Ampere's circuital law), study the forces that a magnetic field exerts on moving charges and on current-carrying conductors, and finally see how these ideas are used in a moving-coil galvanometer and how such a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter or a voltmeter.

16.1 OERSTED'S EXPERIMENT

Oersted placed a magnetic compass below a straight wire that lay along the north-south direction. When no current flowed, the needle stayed parallel to the wire. When a current was switched on, the needle turned and tried to set itself PERPENDICULAR to the wire; reversing the current reversed the deflection. The conclusions are:
 (a) An electric current produces a magnetic field around it.
 (b) The magnetic field lines around a straight wire are CONCENTRIC CIRCLES centred on the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to it.
 (c) The direction of the field is given by the RIGHT-HAND THUMB RULE: if the right thumb points along the current, the curled fingers give the direction of B.

16.2 THE BIOT-SAVART LAW

To calculate the field of a current of any shape we imagine the wire divided into tiny elements. The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field dB produced at a point P by a small current element of length dl carrying current I, when the element is at distance r from P and the line joining it to P makes an angle theta with the element:

   dB = (mu0 / 4 pi) * (I dl sin theta) / r^2

Here mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A is the permeability of free space. The direction of dB is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r (given by dl x r). The total field is the vector sum (integral) of the contributions of all elements. The Biot-Savart law is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law: both fall off as 1/r^2, but the magnetic contribution depends on the angle theta and is directed transverse to r.

16.3 FIELD DUE TO A STRAIGHT CONDUCTOR

Applying the Biot-Savart law to a long straight wire and integrating over its length gives, for a point at perpendicular distance a from an infinitely long straight conductor carrying current I:

   B = mu0 I / (2 pi a)

The field is inversely proportional to the distance a and directly proportional to I; the lines are circles around the wire. For a wire of finite length subtending angles phi1 and phi2 at the point, B = (mu0 I / 4 pi a)(sin phi1 + sin phi2).

Worked example: A long straight wire carries I = 10 A. Find B at a = 5 cm = 0.05 m.
   B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 pi x 0.05) = (2 x 10^-7 x 10)/0.05 = 4 x 10^-5 T = 40 microtesla.

16.4 FIELD DUE TO A CIRCULAR CURRENT LOOP

For a circular loop of radius R carrying current I, the Biot-Savart contributions from all elements add up along the axis. At the CENTRE of the loop the field is

   B = mu0 I / (2 R)

and for a coil of N turns, B = mu0 N I / (2 R). On the axis at distance x from the centre,

   B = mu0 N I R^2 / (2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)).

The loop behaves like a small magnet (a magnetic dipole): one face acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole, decided again by the right-hand rule (if the fingers curl along the current, the thumb points to the north face).

Worked example: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 0.1 m carries 2 A. Field at centre:
   B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 100 x 2)/(2 x 0.1) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 200)/0.2 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1000 = 1.26 x 10^-3 T.

16.5 AMPERE'S CIRCUITAL LAW

Ampere's law is a powerful shortcut for symmetric situations. It states that the line integral of the magnetic field B around any closed loop equals mu0 times the net current I_enclosed passing through the loop:

   sum(B . dl) = mu0 I_enclosed

Applications:
 (i) STRAIGHT WIRE: choosing a circular Amperian loop of radius a around the wire, B is constant and tangential, so B (2 pi a) = mu0 I, giving B = mu0 I/(2 pi a) - the same result as the Biot-Savart integration, obtained far more quickly.
 (ii) SOLENOID: a solenoid is a long coil of closely wound turns. Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform and parallel to the axis; outside it is nearly zero. Applying Ampere's law to a rectangular loop gives

   B = mu0 n I

where n is the number of turns per unit length (n = N/L). The solenoid is the electromagnetic analogue of a bar magnet.
 (iii) TOROID: a toroid is a solenoid bent into a ring. Inside a toroid of N turns and mean radius r, B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r); the field is confined entirely within the core and is zero outside.

16.6 FORCE ON A MOVING CHARGE - THE LORENTZ FORCE

A charge q moving with velocity v through a magnetic field B experiences a force

   F = q v B sin theta

where theta is the angle between v and B. In vector form F = q (v x B). Key features:
 - The force is zero when the charge is stationary (v = 0) or moves parallel to B (theta = 0 or 180).
 - The force is maximum, F = q v B, when v is perpendicular to B (theta = 90).
 - The force is always perpendicular to v, so it does NO WORK and cannot change the speed (or kinetic energy) of the charge - only its direction.
When both electric and magnetic fields are present the total force is the full LORENTZ FORCE F = q(E + v x B).

Motion of a charge in a uniform magnetic field: if v is perpendicular to B, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force and the charge moves in a CIRCLE. Setting q v B = m v^2/r,

   r = m v / (q B)

The period T = 2 pi m/(q B) is independent of the speed. If v has a component along B as well, the path is a helix. This principle is used in the cyclotron and in mass spectrometers.

Worked example: A proton (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg) moves at v = 1.0 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T. Radius of its path:
   r = (1.67 x 10^-27 x 1.0 x 10^6)/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.5) = (1.67 x 10^-21)/(0.8 x 10^-19) = 2.09 x 10^-2 m ~ 2.1 cm.

16.7 FORCE ON A CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR

A conductor is full of moving charges, so a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force. For a straight wire of length L carrying current I in a field B, with theta the angle between the wire and B,

   F = B I L sin theta

In vector form F = I (L x B). The direction is given by FLEMING'S LEFT-HAND RULE: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; forefinger points along B (field), middle finger along I (current), and the thumb then gives the direction of the force (thrust). The force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel.

16.8 FORCE BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL CURRENTS - DEFINITION OF THE AMPERE

Each of two long parallel wires sits in the magnetic field of the other, so they exert forces on each other. Wire 1 carrying I1 produces at wire 2 (distance d away) a field B1 = mu0 I1/(2 pi d). The force per unit length on wire 2 is

   F/L = mu0 I1 I2 / (2 pi d)

Currents in the SAME direction ATTRACT; currents in OPPOSITE directions REPEL. This relation defines the ampere: one ampere is that steady current which, flowing in each of two infinitely long parallel wires 1 metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 x 10^-7 newton per metre of length between them (since mu0/(2 pi) x 1 x 1 / 1 = 2 x 10^-7 N/m).

16.9 TORQUE ON A CURRENT LOOP

Place a rectangular coil of N turns, area A, carrying current I, in a uniform field B. The forces on opposite sides form a couple that tries to rotate the coil. The torque is

   tau = N B I A sin theta

where theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the coil (or, equivalently, tau = N B I A cos alpha where alpha is the angle between the plane of the coil and B). The torque is maximum (tau = N B I A) when the plane of the coil is PARALLEL to the field, and zero when the plane is perpendicular to the field. The quantity m = N I A is the MAGNETIC MOMENT of the coil, so tau = m B sin theta.

16.10 THE MOVING-COIL GALVANOMETER

A moving-coil galvanometer uses this torque to detect small currents. A coil is suspended in the field of a permanent magnet with concave (curved) pole pieces and a soft-iron core, which together make the field RADIAL. In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so sin theta = 1 and the deflecting torque is simply N B I A for any position. A spring provides a restoring torque proportional to the deflection, k*phi. At equilibrium N B I A = k phi, so

   phi = (N B A / k) I,   i.e. phi is proportional to I.

The deflection is directly proportional to the current, giving a linear scale. The current sensitivity is phi/I = N B A/k.

16.11 CONVERSION OF A GALVANOMETER

A galvanometer coil can carry only a very small current I_g (its full-scale deflection current) and has a resistance G.

(a) AMMETER (measures large currents): connect a small resistance S, the SHUNT, in PARALLEL with the galvanometer. The shunt carries most of the current. If the ammeter is to read a maximum current I, then the current through the shunt is (I - I_g) and the voltage across both is equal:

   I_g G = (I - I_g) S,   so   S = I_g G / (I - I_g).

Because S is small, an ammeter has a very LOW resistance and is connected in SERIES in a circuit.

(b) VOLTMETER (measures potential difference): connect a high resistance R in SERIES with the galvanometer. To read up to a maximum voltage V,

   V = I_g (G + R),   so   R = V/I_g - G.

Because R is large, a voltmeter has a very HIGH resistance and is connected in PARALLEL across the component whose voltage is to be measured. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.

Worked example (shunt): A galvanometer of resistance G = 50 ohm gives full-scale deflection for I_g = 2 mA. To convert it into an ammeter reading up to 5 A:
   S = I_g G/(I - I_g) = (2 x 10^-3 x 50)/(5 - 2 x 10^-3) = 0.1/4.998 ~ 0.02 ohm.

SUMMARY

- Oersted showed a current produces a magnetic field; the field of a straight wire forms concentric circles (right-hand thumb rule).
- Biot-Savart law: dB = (mu0/4 pi)(I dl sin theta)/r^2.
- Straight wire: B = mu0 I/(2 pi a); circular loop at centre: B = mu0 N I/(2 R).
- Ampere's law sum(B.dl) = mu0 I_enclosed; solenoid B = mu0 n I; toroid B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r).
- Force on a moving charge: F = q v B sin theta; circular path radius r = m v/(q B); period independent of speed. The magnetic force does no work.
- Force on a conductor: F = B I L sin theta (Fleming's left-hand rule).
- Parallel currents: F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d); like currents attract, unlike repel; this defines the ampere.
- Torque on a coil: tau = N B I A sin theta; magnetic moment m = N I A.
- Moving-coil galvanometer: radial field gives phi proportional to I. Convert to ammeter with a small parallel shunt S = I_g G/(I - I_g); to voltmeter with a large series resistance R = V/I_g - G.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Magnetic Effect of Electric Current
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Take mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A. Show your working for numerical problems and state the direction where asked.

questions.question: State the Biot-Savart law and write its mathematical form. Give the direction of dB.
questions.answer: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field dB produced at a point by a small current element I dl. Its magnitude is dB = (mu0/4 pi)(I dl sin theta)/r^2, where r is the distance from the element to the point and theta is the angle between the element dl and the line joining it to the point. The direction of dB is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r (given by dl x r), i.e. given by the right-hand rule. It is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law and falls off as 1/r^2.
questions.explanation: Statement, formula and direction of the Biot-Savart law.

questions.question: A long straight wire carries a current of 8 A. Calculate the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance of 4 cm from the wire.
questions.answer:
Use B = mu0 I/(2 pi a) with I = 8 A and a = 0.04 m.
B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 8)/(2 pi x 0.04) = (2 x 10^-7 x 8)/0.04 = (1.6 x 10^-6)/0.04 = 4 x 10^-5 T = 40 microtesla.
The field lines are circles around the wire; direction by the right-hand thumb rule.
questions.explanation: Direct use of B = mu0 I/(2 pi a).

questions.question: A circular coil of 200 turns and radius 0.05 m carries a current of 3 A. Find the magnetic field at its centre.
questions.explanation: Use B = mu0 N I/(2 R) at the centre of a coil.

questions.question: A solenoid 0.4 m long has 800 turns and carries a current of 2.5 A. Find the magnetic field inside it.
questions.answer:
n = N/L = 800/0.4 = 2000 turns per metre. Inside a long solenoid B = mu0 n I.
B = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000 x 2.5 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 5000 = 2 x 10^-3 pi = 6.28 x 10^-3 T.
So B ~ 6.3 x 10^-3 T, uniform and directed along the axis.
questions.explanation: Use B = mu0 n I with n = N/L for a solenoid.

questions.question: An electron enters a magnetic field of 0.2 T with a speed of 3 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to the field. Calculate the magnetic force on it.
questions.answer:
F = q v B sin theta with theta = 90, so sin theta = 1.
F = (1.6 x 10^-19)(3 x 10^6)(0.2) = 1.6 x 3 x 0.2 x 10^-13 = 0.96 x 10^-13 = 9.6 x 10^-14 N.
The force is perpendicular to the velocity, so the electron moves in a circular path.
questions.explanation: Direct use of F = q v B sin theta at theta = 90.

questions.question: A proton (mass 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, charge 1.6 x 10^-19 C) moves at 2 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. (a) Find the radius of its circular path. (b) Find the period of revolution. (c) Explain why the magnetic force does no work.
questions.answer:
(a) The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: q v B = m v^2/r, so r = m v/(q B).
r = (1.67 x 10^-27 x 2 x 10^6)/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.5) = (3.34 x 10^-21)/(0.8 x 10^-19) = 4.18 x 10^-2 m ~ 4.2 cm.
(b) T = 2 pi m/(q B) = 2 pi (1.67 x 10^-27)/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.5) = 2 pi (1.67 x 10^-27)/(0.8 x 10^-19) = 2 pi x 2.09 x 10^-8 = 1.31 x 10^-7 s.
The period is independent of speed.
(c) The magnetic force F = q(v x B) is always perpendicular to the velocity v. Work done = F.d = F v cos 90 = 0, so the force does no work and cannot change the kinetic energy or speed - it only changes the direction, producing circular motion.
questions.explanation: r = m v/(q B), T = 2 pi m/(q B); force perpendicular to v does no work.

questions.question: A straight wire of length 0.5 m carrying 4 A lies perpendicular to a field of 0.3 T. Find the force on it and give its direction rule.
questions.answer:
F = B I L sin theta with theta = 90.
F = 0.3 x 4 x 0.5 x 1 = 0.6 N.
The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule: forefinger along B, middle finger along the current I, and the thumb then points along the force.
questions.explanation: F = B I L sin theta and Fleming's left-hand rule.

questions.question: Two long parallel wires 2 cm apart carry currents of 5 A and 10 A in the same direction. Find the force per metre between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.
questions.answer:
F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 5 x 10)/(2 pi x 0.02) = (2 x 10^-7 x 50)/0.02 = (1.0 x 10^-5)/0.02 = 5 x 10^-4 N/m.
Because the currents are in the same direction, the force is ATTRACTIVE.
questions.explanation: F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d); like currents attract.

questions.question: Explain, with a diagram description, the working of a moving-coil galvanometer. Why is a radial magnetic field used, and how is the deflection related to the current?
questions.answer:
A moving-coil galvanometer has a rectangular coil of N turns wound on a light frame, suspended between the concave (curved) pole pieces of a permanent magnet, with a soft-iron cylindrical core inside the coil. When a current I flows, the coil experiences a deflecting torque tau = N B I A. A phosphor-bronze suspension (or spring) provides a restoring torque k*phi proportional to the deflection.
The curved pole pieces and iron core make the field RADIAL, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B whatever the deflection; hence sin theta = 1 always and the torque N B I A does not depend on the position of the coil. This gives a linear scale.
At equilibrium the deflecting and restoring torques balance: N B I A = k phi, so phi = (N B A/k) I. The deflection phi is directly proportional to the current I, allowing the current to be read directly. The current sensitivity is phi/I = N B A/k.
questions.explanation: Radial field keeps torque = N B I A for all positions, giving phi proportional to I.

questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 40 ohm shows full-scale deflection at 5 mA. Find the shunt resistance needed to convert it into an ammeter reading up to 2 A.
questions.answer:
For a shunt in parallel: I_g G = (I - I_g) S, so S = I_g G/(I - I_g).
I_g = 5 x 10^-3 A, G = 40 ohm, I = 2 A.
S = (5 x 10^-3 x 40)/(2 - 5 x 10^-3) = 0.2/1.995 = 0.1003 ohm ~ 0.10 ohm.
The small shunt carries most of the current, and the ammeter has a low resistance.
questions.explanation: S = I_g G/(I - I_g) for ammeter conversion.

questions.question: State the conclusions of Oersted's experiment.
questions.answer: A current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle, showing that (1) an electric current produces a magnetic field around it; (2) the field lines are concentric circles around a straight wire, in planes perpendicular to it; and (3) the direction of the field is given by the right-hand thumb rule and reverses when the current reverses.
questions.explanation: Three key conclusions of Oersted.

questions.question: State the Biot-Savart law and compare it with Coulomb's law.
questions.answer: The Biot-Savart law gives the field of a current element: dB = (mu0/4 pi)(I dl sin theta)/r^2, directed perpendicular to the plane of dl and r. Like Coulomb's law it is an inverse-square law (both go as 1/r^2) and both involve a source element. Differences: Coulomb's field is produced by a static charge and points along r (radial), whereas the Biot-Savart field is produced by a current element and points transverse to r (perpendicular to dl and r); the Biot-Savart contribution also depends on the angle theta.
questions.explanation: Statement plus similarities and differences with Coulomb's law.

questions.question: State the right-hand thumb rule for the field around a straight wire.
questions.answer: If the wire is grasped in the right hand with the thumb pointing along the direction of the conventional current, the curled fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field lines, which form concentric circles around the wire.
questions.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule.

questions.question: A long straight wire carries 12 A. Find the magnetic field at 6 cm from it.
questions.answer: B = mu0 I/(2 pi a) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 12)/(2 pi x 0.06) = (2 x 10^-7 x 12)/0.06 = (2.4 x 10^-6)/0.06 = 4 x 10^-5 T = 40 microtesla. The field lines circle the wire; direction by the right-hand thumb rule.
questions.explanation: Use B = mu0 I/(2 pi a).

questions.question: Find the field at the centre of a 50-turn coil of radius 0.2 m carrying 4 A.
questions.explanation: Use B = mu0 N I/(2 R).

questions.question: Explain why a current loop is called a magnetic dipole.
questions.answer: The field pattern of a small current loop is exactly like that of a tiny bar magnet: field lines leave one face (the north pole) and enter the other (the south pole). The face from which the fingers of the right hand emerge (when they curl along the current) is the north face. Because it has a north and south pole and a magnetic moment m = N I A, the loop is called a magnetic dipole.
questions.explanation: Loop has two poles like a bar magnet.

questions.question: State Ampere's circuital law and use it to find the field of a long straight wire.
questions.answer: Ampere's law: the line integral of B around any closed loop equals mu0 times the net current enclosed, sum(B.dl) = mu0 I_enclosed. For a long straight wire choose a circular Amperian loop of radius a centred on the wire. By symmetry B is constant in magnitude and tangential, so sum(B.dl) = B(2 pi a) = mu0 I, giving B = mu0 I/(2 pi a).
questions.explanation: Statement and straight-wire application.

questions.question: A solenoid has 500 turns over 0.25 m and carries 3 A. Find the field inside.
questions.answer: n = N/L = 500/0.25 = 2000 turns/m. B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000 x 3 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 6000 = 7.54 x 10^-3 T. So B ~ 7.5 x 10^-3 T, uniform along the axis.
questions.explanation: Use B = mu0 n I with n = N/L.

questions.question: Why is the magnetic field nearly uniform inside a long solenoid and almost zero outside?
questions.answer: Inside a long, closely-wound solenoid the fields of the individual turns add up to give a strong uniform field parallel to the axis. Outside, the contributions of the turns on opposite sides nearly cancel, spreading over a large region, so the external field is very weak (nearly zero for an ideal long solenoid). Ampere's law confirms B = mu0 n I inside and ~0 outside.
questions.explanation: Fields add inside, cancel outside.

questions.question: A charge of 5 x 10^-6 C moves at 2 x 10^5 m/s perpendicular to a field of 0.4 T. Find the force.
questions.answer: F = q v B sin theta with theta = 90. F = (5 x 10^-6)(2 x 10^5)(0.4)(1) = 5 x 2 x 0.4 x 10^-1 = 4 x 10^-1 = 0.4 N. The force is perpendicular to the velocity.
questions.explanation: Use F = q v B at 90 degrees.

questions.question: Write the Lorentz force and state when the magnetic part is zero.
questions.answer: The Lorentz force is the total force on a charge in electric and magnetic fields: F = q(E + v x B). The magnetic part q(v x B) is zero when (i) the charge is at rest (v = 0), or (ii) the charge moves parallel or antiparallel to B (theta = 0 or 180, so sin theta = 0).
questions.explanation: Lorentz force and conditions for zero magnetic force.

questions.question: Why does the magnetic force never change the speed of a charged particle?
questions.answer: The magnetic force F = q(v x B) is always perpendicular to the velocity v. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work (W = F.d = 0), so it cannot change the kinetic energy and hence the speed. It only changes the direction of the velocity.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular force does no work.

questions.question: An electron (m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) moves at 4 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.25 T. Find the radius of its path.
questions.explanation: Use r = m v/(q B).

questions.question: Show that the time period of a charge circling in a magnetic field is independent of its speed.
questions.answer: For circular motion the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: q v B = m v^2/r, so r = m v/(q B). The period is T = 2 pi r/v = 2 pi (m v/(q B))/v = 2 pi m/(q B). The speed v cancels, so T depends only on m, q and B and not on the speed. (Faster particles travel larger circles in exactly the same time.) This is the principle behind the cyclotron.
questions.explanation: T = 2 pi m/(q B); v cancels.

questions.question: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same magnetic field with the same speed, both perpendicular. Compare their radii.
questions.answer: r = m v/(q B). The alpha particle has mass ~4 times the proton and charge 2 times the proton, so r_alpha/r_proton = (m_alpha/m_proton)/(q_alpha/q_proton) = 4/2 = 2. The alpha particle's circular radius is about twice that of the proton for the same speed and field.
questions.explanation: Ratio of m/q gives radius ratio 2.

questions.question: A 0.4 m wire carries 6 A perpendicular to a field of 0.5 T. Find the force and its direction rule.
questions.answer: F = B I L sin theta = 0.5 x 6 x 0.4 x 1 = 1.2 N. The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule: forefinger along B, middle finger along the current, thumb along the force.
questions.explanation: F = B I L sin theta; Fleming's left-hand rule.

questions.question: State Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.answer: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of the force (thrust) on the conductor.
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule (motor rule).

questions.question: Derive the force per unit length between two long parallel currents and state the rule for attraction/repulsion.
questions.answer: Wire 1 carrying I1 produces at wire 2 (distance d away) a field B1 = mu0 I1/(2 pi d). Wire 2 carries I2 in this field, so the force on a length L is F = B1 I2 L = mu0 I1 I2 L/(2 pi d). Hence the force per unit length is F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d). Currents in the same direction attract; currents in opposite directions repel.
questions.explanation: F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d); like attract, unlike repel.

questions.question: Define the ampere using the force between two parallel wires.
questions.answer: One ampere is that steady current which, flowing in each of two infinitely long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 x 10^-7 newton per metre of length between them.
questions.explanation: SI definition of the ampere.

questions.question: Derive the torque on a rectangular current loop in a uniform magnetic field.
questions.answer: Consider a rectangular coil of N turns, sides of length l and breadth b (area A = l b), carrying current I in a uniform field B. The forces on the two sides of length l are B I l each, equal and opposite, forming a couple. When the normal to the coil makes angle theta with B, the perpendicular distance between these forces is b sin theta, so the torque per turn is (B I l)(b sin theta) = B I A sin theta. For N turns, tau = N B I A sin theta. Writing m = N I A (the magnetic moment), tau = m B sin theta. The torque is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B.
questions.explanation: tau = N B I A sin theta = m B sin theta.

questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 60 ohm gives full-scale deflection at 4 mA. Find the shunt to make it read up to 3 A.
questions.answer: S = I_g G/(I - I_g) = (4 x 10^-3 x 60)/(3 - 4 x 10^-3) = 0.24/2.996 = 0.0801 ohm ~ 0.08 ohm. This small shunt in parallel carries almost all the current.
questions.explanation: Use S = I_g G/(I - I_g).

questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 100 ohm gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. Find the series resistance to convert it into a voltmeter reading up to 5 V.
questions.answer: R = V/I_g - G = 5/(1 x 10^-3) - 100 = 5000 - 100 = 4900 ohm. This large series resistance gives the voltmeter a high resistance so it can be connected in parallel across a component.
questions.explanation: Use R = V/I_g - G.

questions.question: Describe Oersted's experiment and explain how it links electricity and magnetism. Include the direction rule.
questions.answer:
Oersted placed a magnetic compass beneath a straight wire aligned north-south. With no current, the needle stayed parallel to the wire. When a current was passed, the needle turned and tried to set itself perpendicular to the wire; reversing the current reversed the deflection, and increasing the current increased the deflection.
Interpretation: a current produces a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it. The direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule: grasp the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current, and the curled fingers show the field direction.
Significance: before 1820 electricity and magnetism were separate subjects. Oersted's discovery showed that moving charges (currents) create magnetic fields, unifying the two and starting the science of electromagnetism, later completed by Ampere, Faraday and Maxwell.
questions.explanation: Experiment, observations, field pattern, direction rule and significance.

questions.question: Using the Biot-Savart law, obtain the magnetic field at the centre of a circular current loop of radius R with N turns. Then compute B for N = 100, R = 0.1 m, I = 2 A.
questions.answer:
For a circular loop, every current element I dl is at distance R from the centre and is perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre (theta = 90, sin theta = 1). By Biot-Savart, each element contributes dB = (mu0/4 pi)(I dl)/R^2, and all contributions point along the axis in the same direction. Summing over the whole loop, sum(dl) = 2 pi R (the circumference):
B = (mu0/4 pi)(I/R^2)(2 pi R) = mu0 I/(2 R).
For N turns, B = mu0 N I/(2 R).
Numerical: B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 100 x 2)/(2 x 0.1) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 200)/0.2 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1000 = 4 pi x 10^-4 = 1.26 x 10^-3 T. So B ~ 1.26 millitesla along the axis.
questions.explanation: Derivation of B = mu0 N I/(2 R) and numerical evaluation.

questions.question: State Ampere's circuital law and use it to derive the magnetic field inside a long solenoid. What is the field just outside?
questions.answer: Ampere's law: sum(B.dl) = mu0 I_enclosed for any closed loop. For a long solenoid with n turns per unit length carrying current I, take a rectangular Amperian loop with one side of length L inside the solenoid (parallel to the axis) and the opposite side far outside where B ~ 0; the two short sides are perpendicular to B and contribute nothing. Then sum(B.dl) = B L (only the inside side contributes). The current enclosed is (nL)I because nL turns pass through the loop, each carrying I. So B L = mu0 n L I, giving B = mu0 n I. The field is uniform inside and directed along the axis. Just outside a long ideal solenoid the field is nearly zero, because the return field spreads over a very large region.
questions.explanation: Ampere's law with a rectangular loop gives B = mu0 n I; outside ~0.

questions.question: Explain the force on a moving charge in a magnetic field. State its magnitude, direction and the special cases, and give the Lorentz force.
questions.answer:
A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences a magnetic force of magnitude F = q v B sin theta, where theta is the angle between v and B. In vector form F = q(v x B), so the force is perpendicular to both v and B (its direction can be found by the right-hand rule for v x B, or Fleming's left-hand rule for the equivalent current).
Special cases: (i) if v = 0 or theta = 0/180, then F = 0; (ii) F is maximum (= q v B) when v is perpendicular to B; (iii) because F is always perpendicular to v, it does no work and changes only the direction of motion, not the speed.
When an electric field E is also present, the total force is the Lorentz force F = q(E + v x B). This combined force underlies devices such as the cyclotron, mass spectrometer and velocity selector.
questions.explanation: Magnitude, direction, special cases and the Lorentz force.

questions.question: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it. Show that it moves in a circle, derive the radius and period, and explain why the period does not depend on the speed.
questions.answer:
When a charge q of mass m enters a uniform field B with velocity v perpendicular to B, the magnetic force F = q v B is always perpendicular to v. A constant-magnitude force always perpendicular to the velocity produces uniform circular motion. This magnetic force supplies the centripetal force needed:
q v B = m v^2/r  =>  r = m v/(q B).
So the radius is proportional to the momentum m v and inversely proportional to q B.
The period is T = circumference/speed = 2 pi r/v = 2 pi (m v/(q B))/v = 2 pi m/(q B). The speed cancels, so T (and the frequency f = q B/(2 pi m), called the cyclotron frequency) is independent of the speed and of the radius: faster particles simply move on larger circles and cover them in the same time. Since the magnetic force does no work, the speed and kinetic energy stay constant throughout the circular motion.
questions.explanation: Circular motion, r = m v/(q B), T = 2 pi m/(q B), speed-independent period.

questions.question: Explain the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Give the formula, the direction rule, and a numerical example.
questions.answer:
A current-carrying conductor contains moving charges, each of which feels a magnetic force; the sum is a force on the whole wire. For a straight wire of length L carrying current I in a uniform field B, with theta the angle between the wire and B, the force magnitude is F = B I L sin theta, and in vector form F = I(L x B). The force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to B (theta = 90) and zero when parallel (theta = 0).
Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule - stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; forefinger points along the field, middle finger along the current, and the thumb gives the direction of the force.
Example: a wire of length 0.5 m carrying 4 A perpendicular to a field of 0.3 T feels F = 0.3 x 4 x 0.5 x 1 = 0.6 N. This 'motor effect' is the basis of electric motors and loudspeakers.
questions.explanation: F = B I L sin theta, Fleming's left-hand rule, worked example.

questions.question: Explain the force between two long parallel current-carrying wires, derive the force per unit length, and show how it defines the ampere.
questions.answer:
Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other. Wire 1 carrying I1 produces at wire 2 (distance d) a field B1 = mu0 I1/(2 pi d) directed by the right-hand rule. Wire 2, carrying I2 in this field, feels a force per length F/L = B1 I2 = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d). By Newton's third law wire 1 feels an equal and opposite force. If the currents are parallel (same direction) the wires attract; if antiparallel they repel.
Definition of the ampere: set I1 = I2 = 1 A and d = 1 m in vacuum. Then F/L = (4 pi x 10^-7)/(2 pi) x 1 x 1/1 = 2 x 10^-7 N/m. So one ampere is the steady current that, flowing in each of two infinitely long parallel wires 1 metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 x 10^-7 newton per metre between them.
questions.explanation: F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d); the ampere from F/L = 2 x 10^-7 N/m.

questions.question: Describe the moving-coil galvanometer and explain how it is converted into (a) an ammeter and (b) a voltmeter, with the relevant formulas.
questions.answer:
A moving-coil galvanometer has a coil of N turns and area A suspended in the radial field B of a permanent magnet (curved pole pieces plus a soft-iron core). A current I gives a deflecting torque N B I A; because the field is radial the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so the torque is N B I A for any deflection. A spring gives a restoring torque k phi. At balance N B I A = k phi, so phi = (N B A/k) I - the deflection is proportional to the current, giving a linear scale.
(a) AMMETER: the coil carries only a small full-scale current I_g and has resistance G. To read up to current I, connect a small resistance S (the shunt) in parallel so the extra current (I - I_g) bypasses the coil. Equal voltages give I_g G = (I - I_g) S, so S = I_g G/(I - I_g). Because S is small the ammeter has low resistance and is placed in series in the circuit.
(b) VOLTMETER: connect a large resistance R in series with the galvanometer. To read up to voltage V, V = I_g (G + R), so R = V/I_g - G. Because R is large the voltmeter has high resistance and is placed in parallel across the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.
questions.explanation: Galvanometer principle; ammeter shunt S = I_g G/(I - I_g); voltmeter R = V/I_g - G.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1820 Oersted found that a compass needle placed near a straight current-carrying wire is deflected. The magnetic field of the wire forms concentric circles around it, and the Biot-Savart law dB = (mu0/4 pi)(I dl sin theta)/r^2 gives the field of any small current element.

(i) What does Oersted's experiment prove?
(ii) What shape are the field lines around a straight wire?
(iii) On what quantities does dB in the Biot-Savart law depend?
(iv) What rule gives the direction of the field around the wire?
questions.answer:
(i) It proves that an electric current produces a magnetic field around it (electricity and magnetism are linked).
(ii) The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it.
(iii) dB is proportional to the current I, the element length dl and sin theta, and inversely proportional to r^2 (dB = (mu0/4 pi) I dl sin theta/r^2).
(iv) The right-hand thumb rule: thumb along the current, curled fingers along the field.
questions.explanation: Covers Oersted's result, field pattern, Biot-Savart dependence and the direction rule.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A circular coil of 80 turns has a radius of 0.05 m and carries a current of 5 A. The field at the centre of a coil is B = mu0 N I/(2 R), and the coil acts like a magnetic dipole.

(i) Write the formula for the field at the centre.
(ii) Calculate the field at the centre for the given data.
(iii) What happens to the field if the number of turns is doubled?
(iv) Why is the coil called a magnetic dipole?
questions.answer:
(i) B = mu0 N I/(2 R).
(ii) B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 80 x 5)/(2 x 0.05) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 400)/0.1 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 4000 = 5.03 x 10^-3 T ~ 5.0 millitesla.
(iii) Doubling N doubles the field (B is proportional to N), giving about 1.0 x 10^-2 T.
(iv) Its field pattern has a north face and a south face like a small bar magnet, with magnetic moment m = N I A.
questions.explanation: Applies B = mu0 N I/(2 R) with numerical and conceptual parts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ampere's circuital law sum(B.dl) = mu0 I_enclosed lets us find fields in symmetric situations. A solenoid 0.5 m long has 1000 turns and carries 2 A.

(i) State Ampere's circuital law.
(ii) Find n, the number of turns per metre.
(iii) Calculate the field inside the solenoid.
(iv) What is the field just outside the solenoid?
questions.answer:
(i) The line integral of B around a closed loop equals mu0 times the net current enclosed: sum(B.dl) = mu0 I_enclosed.
(ii) n = N/L = 1000/0.5 = 2000 turns per metre.
(iii) B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000 x 2 = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 4000 = 5.03 x 10^-3 T ~ 5.0 millitesla.
(iv) For a long ideal solenoid the field just outside is nearly zero.
questions.explanation: Ampere's law statement plus solenoid field calculation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A charge experiences a magnetic force F = q v B sin theta, part of the Lorentz force F = q(E + v x B). An alpha particle (charge 3.2 x 10^-19 C) moves at 5 x 10^5 m/s perpendicular to a field of 0.2 T.

(i) Write the Lorentz force expression.
(ii) Calculate the magnetic force on the alpha particle.
(iii) In which direction is this force relative to the velocity?
(iv) When would this magnetic force be zero?
questions.answer:
(i) F = q(E + v x B).
(ii) F = q v B sin 90 = (3.2 x 10^-19)(5 x 10^5)(0.2)(1) = 3.2 x 5 x 0.2 x 10^-14 = 3.2 x 10^-14 N.
(iii) The force is perpendicular to the velocity (and to B).
(iv) It would be zero if the particle were at rest (v = 0) or moved parallel/antiparallel to B (theta = 0 or 180).
questions.explanation: Lorentz force, numerical magnitude, direction and zero conditions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A proton (m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) enters a uniform field of 0.4 T at 3 x 10^6 m/s perpendicular to the field. It moves in a circle because the magnetic force provides the centripetal force.

(i) Write the expression for the radius of the path.
(ii) Calculate the radius.
(iii) Calculate the period of revolution.
(iv) Why does the magnetic force not change the proton's speed?
questions.answer:
(i) r = m v/(q B).
(ii) r = (1.67 x 10^-27 x 3 x 10^6)/(1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.4) = (5.01 x 10^-21)/(6.4 x 10^-20) = 7.8 x 10^-2 m ~ 7.8 cm.
(iii) T = 2 pi m/(q B) = 2 pi (1.67 x 10^-27)/(6.4 x 10^-20) = 2 pi x 2.61 x 10^-8 = 1.64 x 10^-7 s.
(iv) Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work; it changes only the direction, not the speed or kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: r = m v/(q B), T = 2 pi m/(q B), no work done.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is F = B I L sin theta, with direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule. A wire of length 0.6 m carries 5 A in a field of 0.3 T.

(i) Write the formula and its vector form.
(ii) Calculate the force when the wire is perpendicular to the field.
(iii) What is the force when the wire is parallel to the field?
(iv) State Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.answer:
(i) F = B I L sin theta; vector form F = I(L x B).
(ii) At theta = 90, F = 0.3 x 5 x 0.6 x 1 = 0.9 N.
(iii) At theta = 0 (parallel), sin theta = 0, so F = 0.
(iv) Hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular: forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current, and the thumb gives the direction of the force.
questions.explanation: F = B I L sin theta with the two limiting cases and Fleming's rule.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two long parallel wires carry currents I1 and I2 separated by distance d. Each is in the field of the other, giving a force per unit length F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d). This force defines the ampere. Take I1 = 6 A, I2 = 4 A, d = 3 cm.

(i) Write the formula for force per unit length.
(ii) Calculate F/L for the given data.
(iii) If the currents are in the same direction, is the force attractive or repulsive?
(iv) State the definition of the ampere.
questions.answer:
(i) F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d).
(ii) F/L = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 6 x 4)/(2 pi x 0.03) = (2 x 10^-7 x 24)/0.03 = (4.8 x 10^-6)/0.03 = 1.6 x 10^-4 N/m.
(iii) Same-direction currents attract.
(iv) One ampere is the current that, in each of two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 x 10^-7 N per metre between them.
questions.explanation: Parallel-current force, numerical value, attraction rule and ampere definition.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A coil in a magnetic field feels a torque tau = N B I A sin theta. A moving-coil galvanometer uses a radial field so that the deflection is proportional to the current. A coil has N = 50 turns, area A = 2 x 10^-4 m^2, in a field B = 0.1 T, carrying 10 mA.

(i) Write the torque formula.
(ii) Calculate the maximum torque on the coil.
(iii) Why is a radial field used in a galvanometer?
(iv) What is the magnetic moment of the coil?
questions.answer:
(i) tau = N B I A sin theta.
(ii) Maximum torque (sin theta = 1): tau = 50 x 0.1 x (10 x 10^-3) x (2 x 10^-4) = 50 x 0.1 x 0.01 x 2 x 10^-4 = 1.0 x 10^-6 N m.
(iii) A radial field keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to B, so sin theta = 1 for every position; the torque is N B I A throughout, making the deflection directly proportional to the current and the scale linear.
(iv) Magnetic moment m = N I A = 50 x 0.01 x 2 x 10^-4 = 1.0 x 10^-4 A m^2.
questions.explanation: Torque formula, numerical torque, radial-field reason and magnetic moment.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A galvanometer has resistance G = 50 ohm and gives full-scale deflection at I_g = 2 mA. It can be converted into an ammeter with a shunt S = I_g G/(I - I_g) or into a voltmeter with a series resistance R = V/I_g - G.

(i) Find the shunt needed to read up to 1 A.
(ii) Find the series resistance needed to read up to 5 V.
(iii) Which instrument has low resistance and which has high resistance?
(iv) How is each connected in a circuit?
questions.answer:
(i) S = I_g G/(I - I_g) = (2 x 10^-3 x 50)/(1 - 2 x 10^-3) = 0.1/0.998 = 0.10 ohm.
(ii) R = V/I_g - G = 5/(2 x 10^-3) - 50 = 2500 - 50 = 2450 ohm.
(iii) The ammeter (with the small shunt) has low resistance; the voltmeter (with the large series resistance) has high resistance.
(iv) The ammeter is connected in series with the circuit; the voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component.
questions.explanation: Shunt and series-resistance calculations plus connection rules.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A toroid is a solenoid bent into a ring. Inside a toroid of N turns and mean radius r the field is B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r), confined to the core with zero field outside. A toroid has 3000 turns, mean radius 0.10 m and carries 2 A.

(i) Write the formula for the field inside a toroid.
(ii) Calculate the field inside for the given data.
(iii) What is the field outside the toroid?
(iv) How does a toroid differ from a straight solenoid in the way the field is confined?
questions.answer:
(i) B = mu0 N I/(2 pi r).
(ii) B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 3000 x 2)/(2 pi x 0.10) = (2 x 10^-7 x 3000 x 2)/0.10 = (1.2 x 10^-3)/0.10 = 1.2 x 10^-2 T.
(iii) The field outside a toroid is zero.
(iv) A straight solenoid has a uniform field inside and a weak return field spread outside through open ends; a toroid closes on itself so the field is completely confined within the ring core, with essentially none outside.
questions.explanation: Toroid field formula, numerical value and confinement comparison.
